stories.headline: Witkoff and Kushner land in Moscow for US talks
stories.dek: Their plane arrived at Vnukovo Airport at 12:52 p.m. Moscow time, where Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev met them on the tarmac.
paragraphs: US envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on Friday for consultations with Russian officials. Their plane landed at Vnukovo Airport at 12:52 p.m. local time. The visit matters because the Kremlin says talks with the US side are due to take place soon.

Witkoff serves as a special presidential envoy, and Kushner is Donald Trump’s son-in-law and a former White House adviser. Russian state media said Kirill Dmitriev, who handles investment and economic cooperation, met them at the airport. President Vladimir Putin had said earlier they would be welcome in Russia.

The agenda, length and level of the meetings are still unclear. The Kremlin has said it will brief reporters only after consultations happen. It is also not clear whether the talks will cover Ukraine, sanctions, business ties or a broader attempt to reopen regular contact between Moscow and Washington.
stories.changes: It signals that direct high-level contact between US and Russian figures is active again, and more details from Moscow may follow soon.
stories.unchanged: This arrival alone does not mean any agreement has been reached or that US-Russia relations have materially improved.

cover.title: Witkoff and Kushner in Moscow
cover.standfirst: The two US negotiators landed at Vnukovo Airport at 12:52 p.m. Moscow time on Friday. Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev met them on arrival.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: Draw the Vnukovo airport tarmac with a white business jet just stopped, its stairs lowered. At the foot of the stairs stand two anonymous suited figures carrying document folders, greeted by a third suited official beside a black government sedan, with Moscow’s skyline faint in the background. No faces should be detailed.
art.note: Tense but orderly; bold reds, slate blue, cream.

stories.headline: U.S. envoys arrive in Moscow as air war intensifies
stories.dek: Ukraine said it would pause airstrikes during the visit, but Russia gave no public answer and attacks continued overnight.
paragraphs: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on Saturday to restart stalled talks on ending Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The trip comes as both countries step up drone and missile attacks. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine would halt airstrikes during the visit and asked Russia to do the same.

The war is now in its fifth year, and recent U.S. diplomacy has slowed as Washington focused on its conflict with Iran. Russia has been hitting Kyiv and other cities with heavier air attacks, while Ukraine has kept striking targets inside Russia. Front-line fighting has moved little, so the air war has become more central.

There is no sign yet that the Moscow visit will produce a ceasefire or fresh talks. Russia did not publicly answer Ukraine's proposal for a pause in air attacks. Zelenskyy said he expected the U.S. envoys in Kyiv on Sunday, but it remains unclear whether either side is ready to change its war aims.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this means the U.S. is trying again to push direct diplomacy even as fighting continues.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean a ceasefire is in place or that the war is close to ending.

cover.title: U.S. Envoys Reach Moscow
cover.standfirst: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived on Saturday to revive peace efforts over Ukraine. Kyiv offered to pause airstrikes during the visit, but Russian attacks continued overnight.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: Draw a dark airport tarmac in Moscow with a parked government jet in the background and two unmarked suited figures descending mobile stairs, seen only from behind. Above them, the sky splits into two layers: one side filled with small fast drones and the other with the faint outline of Kyiv apartment blocks and a damaged warehouse, linking diplomacy and the ongoing air war in one frame.
art.note: Grave, tense mood; deep blacks, bruised red, cold gray-blue.

stories.headline: Newcastle host Bournemouth as Premier League returns at St James’ Park
stories.dek: The lunchtime match opened under August sun, with attention on Bournemouth keeping midfielder Alex Scott after the transfer window.
paragraphs: Newcastle United played Bournemouth at St James’ Park in a Premier League lunchtime kickoff on Saturday. The match drew early attention because it was part of the opening stretch of the new season, with both clubs starting again after the summer break and transfer window.

For a new reader, this is a regular-season English top-flight match, not a cup tie. Pre-match coverage focused on the mood inside the ground, the sunny conditions and Bournemouth manager Marco Rose saying he was pleased to keep key players, especially midfielder Alex Scott.

What remains unresolved is the result, the main incidents and how either side actually performed, because only pre-match and live-blog summary details were available. It is also not yet clear whether Bournemouth’s settled squad, or Newcastle’s home advantage, mattered once the game started.
stories.changes: For an ordinary reader, this means the Premier League weekend is under way and both clubs begin adding real points, pressure and evidence.
stories.unchanged: One early match does not settle either club’s season, whatever the mood, transfer talk or predictions before kickoff suggest.

cover.title: Newcastle Face Bournemouth
cover.standfirst: The Premier League lunchtime match kicked off at St James’ Park on Saturday. Pre-match focus fell on Bournemouth keeping midfielder Alex Scott after the summer window.

art.label: Comic absurd
art.concept: Draw St James’ Park in bright August sun with a black-and-white corner flag bending in the breeze and a football balanced exactly on the centre spot. Around it, two sets of empty boots and socks rush in from opposite sides of the pitch, one in Newcastle stripes and one in Bournemouth red and black, to suggest the teams just emerging for kickoff.
art.note: Light, lively, sunny palette with crisp greens and sharp black-and-white contrast.

stories.headline: Local ceasefire starts to repair Zaporizhzhia plant power line
stories.dek: The pause in fighting is meant to let crews fix a damaged line and reconnect the nuclear plant to outside electricity.
paragraphs: A local ceasefire has taken effect near the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency. The pause is meant to let repair crews work on a damaged power line. The goal is to restore the plant’s external electricity supply as quickly as possible.

Zaporizhzhia is Europe’s largest nuclear power plant. Even when its reactors are not producing power, the site still needs steady outside electricity to run cooling and safety systems. Fighting around the plant has repeatedly damaged lines, forcing the facility to rely on backup arrangements that are less secure.

It is not yet clear how long the ceasefire will hold or when the line will be fully repaired. The condition of the wider power network around the plant is also unclear. A single repaired line would reduce immediate risk, but it would not remove the danger from nearby fighting.
stories.changes: For people following the war, this means the plant may soon have a safer and more stable source of electricity.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean the wider war has paused or that the nuclear risk around Zaporizhzhia has ended.

cover.title: Ceasefire at Nuclear Plant
cover.standfirst: A local pause in fighting near Zaporizhzhia began on Sept. 5 to let crews repair a damaged power line. The aim is to restore outside electricity to the plant.

art.label: Decorative flat
art.concept: Draw the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant with its cooling towers and reactor buildings beside a tall damaged transmission pylon. In the foreground, utility workers in hard hats repair sagging power cables while the area around the plant sits unnaturally still, with military earthworks and silent roads at the edge of the frame.
art.note: Tense but clear; muted blue-grey with sharp safety yellow accents.

stories.headline: Sara Duterte posts bail after arrest order in threat case
stories.dek: The Philippine vice president paid 360,000 pesos after a court ordered her arrest over alleged threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
paragraphs: Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail on Saturday after a Quezon City court ordered her arrest a day earlier. She faces three counts of grave threats over remarks in 2024 about having President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and two others killed if she were killed.

Duterte denies threatening the president and says she was speaking about her own safety. The case comes from a public split between two powerful political families that won the 2022 election together. Marcos and Duterte now face each other in court and in a separate Senate impeachment trial.

The criminal case will now move forward while Duterte remains free on bail. A conviction could bar her from public office and damage any 2028 presidential bid. It is still unclear how fast the courts will act, or how much the case will deepen the country's political divide.
stories.changes: This raises the legal and political risk around the Philippine vice president and could affect the next presidential race.
stories.unchanged: She remains vice president for now, and the case does not by itself remove her from office.

cover.title: Sara Duterte Posts Bail
cover.standfirst: The Philippine vice president paid 360,000 pesos in Manila after an arrest order in a grave threats case. Prosecutors cite remarks about President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. made in 2024.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: Draw the steps of a Manila courthouse with a vice-presidential sash draped over an empty black chair at the center. In the foreground, a judge's gavel, a bail receipt stamped with 360,000 pesos, and three shadowy silhouette cutouts stand beside a cluster of police uniforms and microphones, showing the legal and political pressure without depicting any real face.
art.note: Tense and public; hot reds, deep blue, cream paper.

stories.headline: Repairs start on external power line at Zaporozhye plant
stories.dek: The plant said work is under way to bring the Ferrosplavnaya line back into service as soon as possible.
paragraphs: Repair work has started at the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant to restore an external power line, according to a plant statement on Telegram. The site said crews are working on the Ferrosplavnaya line now because the plant needs stable off-site electricity for essential systems.

The Zaporozhye plant is a nuclear facility in southeastern Ukraine that relies on outside power even when its reactors are not generating electricity. External lines keep cooling, monitoring and other safety equipment running. When those lines fail, the plant must depend on backup arrangements such as emergency generators.

It is still not clear when the Ferrosplavnaya line will be fully restored or how reliable the connection will be after repairs. The statement gave no cause for the outage and no timetable beyond saying the line should return to operation as soon as possible.
stories.changes: For people following the plant, this means one key outside power link is being worked on rather than left offline.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean the plant is back to normal or that wider nuclear safety concerns around the site are over.

cover.title: Power Line Repairs Begin
cover.standfirst: Workers at the Zaporozhye nuclear plant have started restoring the Ferrosplavnaya external line. The site said it wants the connection back in service as soon as possible.

art.label: Bold symbol
art.concept: Draw the Zaporozhye nuclear plant as a concrete reactor complex in the background, with one damaged high-voltage transmission line running toward it across open ground. In the foreground, utility workers in hard hats repair a snapped pylon and reconnect thick power cables, while the plant sits dark except for a few lit safety windows.
art.note: Tense but practical; hot orange, steel blue, and dusty grey.

stories.headline: Court convicts 10 Maoists in 2013 Jheeram Valley killings
stories.dek: A special NIA court in Jagdalpur found ten accused guilty in the Sukma ambush that killed senior Congress leaders and many others.
paragraphs: A special NIA court in Jagdalpur has convicted ten Maoist accused in the 2013 Jheeram Valley massacre in Chhattisgarh. The court has not yet announced the sentences. It will decide the punishment on September 16. Defence lawyers said the convicts plan to challenge the verdict in the High Court.

The case comes from a major Maoist attack on May 25, 2013, near Jheeram Valley in Sukma district. A convoy of Congress leaders was returning from a Parivartan Yatra rally when Maoists blasted the road, trapped the vehicles, then opened fire and threw grenades. At least 27 people were killed.

The full case is not over. The NIA had charged 39 members of the banned CPI (Maoist), and this verdict covers ten of them. Questions over the roles of senior Maoist leaders remain. The court still has to fix the sentences, and appeals could take the case into higher courts.
stories.changes: The verdict moves one of India’s deadliest Maoist attack cases from investigation to punishment, after more than a decade.
stories.unchanged: It does not end the wider Maoist conflict in central India, and it does not close every part of the Jheeram Valley case.

cover.title: Jheeram Valley Convictions
cover.standfirst: A special NIA court in Jagdalpur convicted ten Maoist accused in the 2013 Sukma ambush. The attack killed 27 people, including senior Congress leaders. Sentencing is due on September 16.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: Draw a shattered convoy of white SUVs and jeeps halted on a narrow forest road beside a fresh crater blasted into the ground. Dark armed silhouettes emerge from dense sal trees on both sides, while abandoned political rally flags and scattered papers lie around the vehicles. No faces, no text.
art.note: Grave and stark; deep forest greens, mud brown, black, and a hard red accent.

stories.headline: Justice Department widens scrutiny of virus researchers beyond Fauci
stories.dek: A federal inquiry appears to reach past one public figure and into a broader group of scientists tied to pandemic-era research.
paragraphs: The Justice Department is pursuing an investigation involving Dr. Anthony Fauci and other virus scientists, according to the report. The inquiry appears broader than the public fight on Capitol Hill, which has focused heavily on Fauci. It matters now because political pressure around pandemic decisions and research has not faded.

For years, Fauci has been a central target for congressional Republicans over Covid policy, federal funding and research links to virus work. The new report suggests federal investigators have quietly looked beyond him to a wider circle of researchers. That points to a separate track from televised hearings and partisan attacks.

It is still unclear what conduct investigators are examining, how many scientists are involved, or whether any charges are likely. The full scope of the inquiry is not public. It is also unresolved how much this effort overlaps with congressional investigations and whether it concerns research funding, testimony or other actions.
stories.changes: It raises the chance that scrutiny of pandemic-era science will extend beyond hearings and into formal federal investigation.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean Fauci or any other scientist has been charged with a crime or found to have done anything illegal.

cover.title: D.O.J. Scrutiny of Virus Science
cover.standfirst: A reported federal inquiry reaches beyond Anthony Fauci to other researchers tied to pandemic-era work. Key facts remain undisclosed, including scope, subjects and any possible charges.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: Draw a sealed evidence box on a metal table inside a plain federal office. Inside the box are concrete lab objects: stacked petri dishes, a pipette, grant paperwork with blacked-out lines, and a white lab coat on a hanger, while a Department of Justice building seal sits on the wall behind, slightly looming. No people, no faces.
art.note: Tense and institutional; acid yellow, deep navy, dirty white.

stories.headline: Treasury surge squeezes weakest US companies seeking fresh debt
stories.dek: Higher government bond yields and heavy tech borrowing are making refinancing harder for lower-rated American companies.
paragraphs: US Treasury yields have climbed to multi-year highs, pushing up borrowing costs across the market. That is hitting the weakest corporate borrowers first. Lower-rated companies that need to refinance soon now face higher interest bills and less investor appetite, as safer bonds offer better returns.

The 30-year Treasury yield moved above 5.3% and the 10-year reached about 4.8%, levels not seen for years. Yields are rising because the US is issuing more debt, foreign buyers like China hold less, and big tech groups are selling large amounts of bonds to fund AI data centres.

The main unknown is how long yields stay this high. Treasury buybacks have offered only brief relief. If government borrowing stays heavy and major investors keep pulling back, weaker companies could face more defaults, distressed debt swaps, or expensive last-minute refinancing before their bonds mature.
stories.changes: If you own junk-bond funds, work at a heavily indebted company, or need business credit, borrowing may get harder and more expensive.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean most large US companies are in immediate trouble, or that household borrowing costs will jump overnight from this alone.

cover.title: Weak Borrowers Hit the Wall
cover.standfirst: US Treasury yields rose above levels last seen before the financial crisis. Lower-rated companies now face costlier refinancing as tech groups sell billions in new bonds for AI projects.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: Draw a steep wall made from oversized US Treasury bonds, with the weakest corporate borrowers shown as small generic office buildings with cracked facades sliding back down it. At the top, huge glossy bond certificates from major tech companies crowd the path, soaking up investor cash, while a few loose dollar bills and broken ladders fall away below.
art.note: Sharp, tense, high-contrast colours with a hard financial mood.

stories.headline: Telangana announces giant AI data centre for Future City
stories.dek: The ₹70,000 crore project is backed by Tata Group, TCS and HyperVault and is meant to open on June 2, 2028.
paragraphs: Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy said Tata Group, TCS and HyperVault will build a ₹70,000 crore AI data centre in Future City near Hyderabad. He called it the biggest investment yet in the State by TCS. The government wants the project completed by June 2, 2028.

The plan is for a large AI data centre campus with capacity of up to 1 gigawatt. The State says it will be the largest data centre in India and create 7,000 direct jobs. Reddy linked the announcement to talks with Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran in Davos earlier this year.

Key details are still missing. The announcement does not set out the construction phases, power source, water use, land terms or final financing structure. It is also not yet clear how many jobs will be permanent technical roles, or when the first part of the campus will start operating.
stories.changes: If the project goes ahead on schedule, Hyderabad will gain a huge new tech and infrastructure site with thousands of direct jobs.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean the data centre exists yet, or that AI work and hiring in Telangana will change overnight.

cover.title: Future City AI Data Centre
cover.standfirst: Telangana says Tata Group, TCS and HyperVault will build a ₹70,000 crore campus near Hyderabad. The State wants the 1 gigawatt project opened by June 2, 2028.

art.label: Maximalist doodle
art.concept: Draw a vast data centre campus under construction in Future City: long low server buildings, cooling towers, power lines and cranes spreading across a dry open site outside Hyderabad. In the foreground, a ceremonial foundation stone and a hard hat rest beside rolled building plans, while a broad new road curves toward the complex.
art.note: Ambitious and public-facing; hot pink, electric blue and concrete grey.
